conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is well supported and not false, citing strong evidence from a landmark randomized controlled trial and a Cochrane systematic review to endorse the superior efficacy of chlorhexidine-alcohol.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
The claim is well supported, not false.

The landmark evidence is a large multicenter randomized controlled trial (Tuuli et al., NEJM 2016), which found that "the use of chlorhexidine–alcohol for preoperative skin antisepsis resulted in a significantly lower risk of surgical-site infection after cesarean delivery than did the use of iodine–alcohol" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

This finding is corroborated by the 2020 Cochrane systematic review, the gold standard for synthesizing surgical evidence, which concluded with "moderate-certainty evidence" that "preparing the skin with chlorhexidine gluconate before caesarean section is probably slightly more effective at reducing the incidence of surgical site infection in comparison to povidone iodine" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/).

Additional meta-analyses reinforce this direction of effect. A network meta-analysis in the Journal of Hospital Infection found that "alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of being effective in preventing surgical site infections, followed by alcohol-based povidone–iodine" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282). Smaller individual trials, such as a pilot RCT, showed a similar direction of benefit for chlorhexidine that did not reach statistical significance due to limited sample size, which is consistent with—not contradictory to—the larger trial and meta-analytic findings (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/).

While one earlier meta-analysis (Huang et al., 2017) suggested no additional advantage, the totality of evidence—including the large NEJM RCT and the Cochrane review—supports the claim that chlorhexidine-alcohol reduces surgical-site infection compared with iodine-alcohol before cesarean delivery. This is why major bodies like WHO and CDC recommend chlorhexidine-alcohol as the preferred skin antiseptic. The skepticism in the original claim appears unwarranted based on current high-quality evidence.
